---
title: "Total marginal effects in R"
subtitle: "Holistic effect size measures for nominal and ordinal outcome models"
---

In a model with several outcome categories -- a multinomial or ordered logit
or probit, for example -- a predictor has one marginal effect per category,
and no single one of them says how much the predictor matters. The **Total
marginal effect (Total ME)** from Mize and Han (2025) summarizes them in a
single number: the sum of the absolute values of the marginal effects across
all outcome categories, divided by two. That is the total amount of
probability the predictor moves between the categories.

In R, you can calculate it with the
[`marginaleffects`](https://marginaleffects.com/) package, which handles the
marginal effects and the standard errors. For nominal or ordinal predictors,
the [`meineq_weights()`](https://github.com/tdmize/Rfunctions/blob/main/ME_helper_functions.R)
helper calculates the weights for the weighted **Total ME inequality**. The
same measures are available in Stata with the
[`totalme`](/software/totalme/index.qmd) command.

## Setup

`meineq_weights()` is in my `Rfunctions` repository on GitHub. Load it with
`source()`:

```r
library(marginaleffects) # Marginal effects and hypotheses

source("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tdmize/Rfunctions/main/ME_helper_functions.R")
```

## Continuous and binary predictors

Total MEs for several predictors can be calculated in one call:

```r
avg_comparisons(mod,
  variables = list(age = "sd",
                   binaryvar = "reference"),
  hypothesis = ~ I(sum(abs(x)) / 2) | term)
```

`avg_comparisons()` calculates each predictor's marginal effect on every
outcome category. `hypothesis` then adds up the absolute values and divides by
two, separately for each predictor (`| term`).

## Nominal or ordinal predictors

For a nominal predictor, first calculate a Total ME for every pairwise
contrast between its categories (`| contrast`), then average those using the
ME inequality weights:

```r
avg_comparisons(mod,
  variables = list(nominalvar = "pairwise"),
  hypothesis = ~ I(sum(abs(x)) / 2) | contrast) |>
  hypotheses(hypothesis = meineq_weights(mod, nominalvar))
```

The result is the weighted **Total ME inequality**.

## Examples

The examples reproduce the Total ME examples from Mize and Han (2025):

- [Total MEs for a single model](examples/single-model.qmd) (Example 5.2.c):
  continuous and binary predictors of self-rated health.
- [Comparing Total MEs across models](examples/across-models.qmd)
  (Example 5.2.e): testing mediation, with models combined by
  [`suest`](/software/suest_r/index.qmd).
- [Total ME inequalities for nominal independent variables](examples/inequalities.qmd)

## Citation

If you use these measures, please cite:

> Mize, Trenton D. and Bing Han. 2025. "Inequality and Total Effect Summary Measures for Nominal and Ordinal Variables." *Sociological Science* 12:115–157.
